title.narrative: Supporting the Collection of Reliable, Local Data on Political Violence and Protest for Early Warning in Mozambique

description.narrative:
The Overall Objective/Impact of the proposed project is to improve policy and programming around conflict prevention/response and early warning efforts in Mozambique.

The three outcomes of this action are: (1) high-quality, locally-informed data on political violence and protest in Mozambique are collected and published; (2) robust, timely, and policy-relevant analysis on political violence and protest in Mozambique is produced and published; (3) data and analysis reaches international, regional, and local policymakers, stakeholders, and conflict-affected individuals

description.narrative: ACLED successfully met most targets associated with this outcome, significantly exceeding the targets for Indicator 3.1.1, Indicator 3.1.2, and Indicator 3.1.3.Concerning the indicator Number of media mentions of Cabo Ligado analysis on political violence and protest in Mozambique, ACLED data and analysis were cited an average of 195 times per month in various media outlets from 1 January 2023 to 30 June 2024, which was below the target set for this indicator. The shift in conflict dynamics and the decrease in insurgent activity and violence resulted in a redirection of international attention away from the reporting and analysis of the situation in Mozambique.With respect to the indicator Number of engagements/meetings held with stakeholders, Cabo Ligado engaged with key stakeholders through at least 59 meetings, briefings, interviews, and presentations during the implementation period, which significantly exceeds the target of nine by the end of the project. More details on the various meetings and briefings with key stakeholders can be found in subsection B. Activities below, under Activity 3.1.1.Regarding the indicator Number of participants in meetings and public engagements, approximately 400 participants (including 38 women) attended Cabo Ligado public engagements throughout the implementation period, significantly exceeding the target of 45 (30 men and 15 women) by the end of the project.With reference to the indicator Number of meetings held with the European Commission stakeholders, 12 meetings were held with stakeholders from the EC, including FPI, EUTM Mozambique, and the EU Delegation to Mozambique. More details on the meetings with EU stakeholders can be found in subsection B. Activities below, under Activity 3.1.2.ACLED successfully met all the targets associated with this outcome during the implementation period.With reference to the indicator of Number of podcast episodes produced per week in each language, Cabo Ligado produced an average of 40 episodes of the Voz de Cabo Delgado podcast per month in five languages (Portuguese, Kiswahili, Emakwa, Shimakonde, and Kimwani) from 1 January 2023 to 30 June 2024. This indicator largely surpassed the initial target of 35 episodes per month. The podcast episodes, ranging from five to nine minutes in length, provide unbiased and datadriven news and commentary on the Cabo Delgado conflict.Considering the indicator Number of listens per month, the episodes of the Voz de Cabo Delgado podcast received an average of 1,221 listens per month throughout the implementation period. The podcast episodes are distributed through Xipalapala, which broadcasts to a network of at least 29 community radio stations in Northern and Central Mozambique. Additionally, they are available on Plural Medias iono.fm account and shared through various social media channels. With regard to the Podcast outreach strategy produced, the Cabo Ligado team developed and shared the `Voz de Cabo Delgado Podcast Reach Strategy in March 2023. This outreach strategy detailed the distribution plan for Voz de Cabo Delgado podcast episodes to radio stations in northern Mozambique, as well as social media channels and podcast apps.

title.narrative: Objective 1: Highquality, locallyinformed data on political violence and protest in Mozambique are collected and published.

description.narrative: ACLED successfully met the targets for Indicator 1.1 and Indicator 1.1.1. For Indicator 1.2, the total fell slightly below target, as detailed below.Data Collection & PublicationThe Cabo Ligado team maintained Mozambiques dataset and dashboard, publishing realtime data weekly, except during ACLEDs scheduled pauses in August 2023, December 2023, and June 2024. Data collection continued throughout these periods, ensuring uninterrupted reporting. The Cabo Ligado dashboard was regularly updated, providing stakeholders with reliable, uptodate insights.ACLED recorded and verified 793 events of political violence and protest across Mozambique, including 536 in Cabo Delgado (January 2023 June 2024). All data remain publicly accessible via ACLEDs Access Portal.Local Source Coverage40% of Mozambique data came from local sources, rising to 51% in Cabo Delgadoslightly below target due to a surge in overall event reporting, geographic coverage, and sources used. Despite an increase in localsource event production, their share of the total decreased proportionally.Community Reporter (CR) NetworkACLED met most targets for expanding the CR network, with adjustments due to reduced violence in Nampula and Niassa. Efforts to recruit female CRs faced challenges, as shown by the resignation of one female CR in Cabo Delgado.Cabo Delgado CRs: 13 new CRs recruited (2 women), bringing the total to 27 (22 men, 5 women). One female CR resigned, leaving the count slightly below the target of 6.Niassa & Nampula CRs: 2 male CRs recruited. Given the decline in insurgent activity, further recruitment was paused. The team continued monitoring needs for potential adjustments.Training: 15 new CRs trained (11 men, 2 women in Cabo Delgado; 1 man in Niassa, 1 in Nampula), bringing the total to 30 (24 men, 6 women).MozambicanTanzanian Border Stringers: One new stringer was recruited in 2023, totaling two. Due to evolving conflict dynamics, recruitment efforts were paused while monitoring continued.ACLEDs adaptive approach ensured resources were efficiently allocated in response to shifting security dynamics. The CRs played a key role in providing accurate, timely data, contributing to Cabo Ligados analytical depth, particularly in understanding the conflicts impact on marginalized groups, including women and children.

title.narrative: Objective 2: Robust, timely, and policyrelevant analysis on political violence and protest in Mozambique is produced and published.

description.narrative: ACLED surpassed the targets associated with this outcome for all relevant indicators. As explained below, the targets for Indicator 2.1, Indicator 2.1.1, and Indicator 2.1.2 were adjusted to reflect the decision to shift from weekly to fortnightly updates.With respect to the indicator Number of analytical products produced by Cabo Ligado, the Cabo Ligado team published a total of 71 analytical outputs focusing on Mozambique, exceeding the target of 60 set for this indicator. This number includes weekly/fortnightly updates, monthly reports, and actor profiles focused on the key parties to the ongoing conflict. Regarding the indicator Number of weekly reports published per month, an average of approximately three updates were published on the Cabo Ligado website monthly, with a total of 47 updates 25 weekly and 22 fortnightly updates published in English and Portuguese. As of 26 July 2023, Cabo Ligado made the decision to transition from weekly to fortnightly updates. This adjustment was made in response to the evolving conflict dynamics in Cabo Delgado, which saw a decrease in political violence incidents, and to accommodate the publication of actor profiles focusing on key conflict actors.With respect to the indicator Number of monthly reports published, a total of 18 monthly reports on the conflict and political violence situation in Mozambique were published in English and Portuguese on the Cabo Ligado website from 1 January 2023 to 30 June 2024. Additionally, a series of analytical deep dives into the parties of the conflict were produced with six actor profiles focusing on Islamic State Mozambique (ISM), Local Forces, Defense Armed Forces of Mozambique, Police of the Republic of Mozambique, SADC Mission in Mozambique, and Tanzania Peoples Defence Force.

title.narrative: Output 1.1 related to Objective 1: Dataset and dashboard of highquality, locallyinformed data on political violence and protest in Mozambique is maintained.

description.narrative: Progress on Activity 1.1.1: From January 2023 through June 2024, ACLED continued its weekly realtime data collection and coverage of political violence and protest in Mozambique, in line with ACLEDs rigorous methodology and comprehensive sourcing guidelines. Through an extensive and growing network of CRs on the ground, the incidents collected through international, national, and subnational sources by the Mozambique data team were verified and/or enriched, ensuring highquality and comprehensive data. Zitamar News (cobeneficiary) and Mediacoop (local partner) contributed to the verification of events using their own reporters and sources. ACLEDs Mozambique data continued to be integrated into the website and dashboard weekly. The ACLED Africa desk, along with the Cabo Ligado analysts and partner organization staff, contributed to the completion of these activities through a process of collecting and synthesizing information from all Cabo Ligado sources that these collaborators refined into a systematic weekly cycle since the pilot phase of the observatory in May 2020. During the implementation period, ACLED published 536 political disorder events in Cabo Delgado and 793 events nationwide. While over 50% of these events were sourced locally, this was slightly below the target. The increase in local sources and events was offset by a substantial rise in overall events, geographic coverage, and sources during the grant period.Mozambique data were released every week on Mondays, with the only exceptions being ACLEDs twoweek data publication pauses in August 2023 and June 2024, as well as ACLEDs twoweek hiatus in December 2023. In all the above cases, data collection continued throughout the period, and data were published following the publication pauses. All published data on the ACLED website are made publicly accessible, per ACLEDs Terms of Use, via ACLEDs Access Portal. Users are required to register in order to download the data. The personal identifying information collected (name, email) is solely used for controlling access to the data (e.g., to prevent misuse), while information on organizational affiliation and use case is used for impact monitoring and reporting purposes.Progress on Activity 1.1.2: ACLED maintained and regularly updated the Cabo Ligado website and dashboard. The dashboard summarizes key statistics, including a timeline of political violence events, a map of violent incidents in the country, a bar chart spotlighting conflict actors, and event details. It ensures the availability of reliable, uptodate, and easily accessible information on Mozambique for users and stakeholders relying on the platform for insights and analysis. During the implementation period, all analytical outputs, including updates, monthly reports, and actor profiles, were published on the Cabo Ligado website. Updates and monthly reports were made available in both English and Portuguese. The actor profile on ISM was also published on ACLEDs main website as part of the ACLED actor profile series. Additionally, the Cabo Ligado website embeds Voz de Cabo Delgado podcast episodes that are published biweekly. During the implementation period, the Cabo Ligado website averaged over 6,760 views and received around 195 citations per month at the local, national and international levels. Moreover, its newsletter now boasts over 3,330 subscribers. Notably, Cabo Ligados analytical outputs were extensively referenced in various reports by key institutions and think tanks focused on conflict prevention and early warning in Mozambique, as outlined in the Impact section.

title.narrative: Output 1.2 related to Objective 1: Network of Community Reporters (CRs) is maintained and improved by increasing the number of CRs in Cabo Delgado and expanding to new regions (Niassa and Nampula).

description.narrative: Progress on Activity 1.2.1: The Cabo Ligado team continued its recruitment efforts to build on the existing CR network in order to accelerate the incident verification process and acquire complementary information for lessercovered incidents. More specifically, the team recruited 13 new CRs in Cabo Delgado, bringing the total number of CRs covering various districts across the province to 27, including 22 men and five women. In the second year of implementation, particular efforts were made to recruit more women as CRs to strengthen the coverage of genderbased violence. Despite challenges in the Mozambican context, two additional female CRs were recruited and trained. As part of the data collection and verification process, the Cabo Ligado team also flagged incidents of potential human rights violations (notably, violence targeting civilians) within the data collected, in an effort to monitor possible violations committed by the state security forces of Mozambique and other actors. The human rights incidents list was then shared with the FPI regional office in Nairobi.Progress on Activity 1.2.2: From January 2023 to June 2024, the Cabo Ligado team recruited two new CRs in Nampula and Niassa provinces. However, due to a halt in reported insurgencyrelated events in these provinces during the reporting period, the team decided to halt the recruitment of new CRs there to adapt to the trends of political violence. This was communicated to and approved by the FPI regional office in Nairobi. This decision was regularly reviewed, taking into consideration the security situation and the potential need for additional CRs.Progress on Activity 1.2.3: All new and existing CRs received indepth training in information collection and management and were provided with secure means to communicate, including mobile phones and a monthly phone credit stipend. During the implementation period, 15 CRs were trained in information collection and secure communications, bringing the total number of trained CRs to 30, including 24 men and six women. One female CR resigned due to relocation.Progress on Activity 1.2.4: During the implementation period, the Cabo Ligado team expanded the stringer network on the MozambicanTanzanian border with an additional stringer focusing on the Mtwara region. The Cabo Ligado team had identified Mtwara as a gap in its coverage due to a lack of sources across their networks and traditional media coverage. However, due to a decrease in militant activity along the border, the team halted the recruitment of an additional stringer in the Ruvuma region. This decision was communicated to and approved by the FPI regional office in Nairobi. Progress on Activity 1.2.5: From January 2023 to June 2024, CRs and stringers continued to collect and share information with the Cabo Ligado team about the situation in their areas of coverage, including data about specific incidents of political violence and protest. Additionally, CRs and stringers were occasionally asked to investigate particular rumors or trends that analysts picked up on, though solely through means and measures that did not put them at risk and ensure their safety. The recruitment and training of more female CRs aimed to bring a gendersensitive lens to information collection and verification, ultimately improving the coverage of genderbased violence. During the implementation period, the CRs contribution to the work of the observatory was the most valuable in the districts of Macomia, Mocmboa da Praia, Muidumbe, Ancuabe, Quissanga, and Nangade, as they saw the highest frequency of insurgent movements and attacks. CRs in other districts, such as Palma, Mueda, Metuge, Pemba, Ibo, and Montepuez provided essential contextual information on the current socioeconomic situation in their regions and on displaced populations. CRs further reported a decrease in insurgencyrelated events in the Nampula and Niassa provinces during the grant period.

In the second year of implementation, particular efforts were made to recruit more women as CRs to strengthen the coverage of genderbased violence. Despite challenges in the Mozambican context, two additional female CRs were recruited and trained. As part of the data collection and verification process, the Cabo Ligado team also flagged incidents of potential human rights violations (notably, violence targeting civilians) within the data collected, in an effort to monitor possible violations committed by the state security forces of Mozambique and other actors. The human rights incidents list was then shared with the FPI regional office in Nairobi.Progress on Activity 1.2.2: From January 2023 to June 2024, the Cabo Ligado team recruited two new CRs in Nampula and Niassa provinces. However, due to a halt in reported insurgencyrelated events in these provinces during the reporting period, the team decided to halt the recruitment of new CRs there to adapt to the trends of political violence. This was communicated to and approved by the FPI regional office in Nairobi. This decision was regularly reviewed, taking into consideration the security situation and the potential need for additional CRs.Progress on Activity 1.2.3: All new and existing CRs received indepth training in information collection and management and were provided with secure means to communicate, including mobile phones and a monthly phone credit stipend. During the implementation period, 15 CRs were trained in information collection and secure communications, bringing the total number of trained CRs to 30, including 24 men and six women. One female CR resigned due to relocation.Progress on Activity 1.2.4: During the implementation period, the Cabo Ligado team expanded the stringer network on the MozambicanTanzanian border with an additional stringer focusing on the Mtwara region. title.narrative: Output 2.1 related to Objective 2: Robust, timely, and policy relevant analysis on political violence and protest in Mozambique is produced on weekly and monthly bases and made freely available.

description.narrative: Progress on Activity 2.1.1: From January 2023 to June 2024, the Cabo Ligado conflict observatory continued the publication of regular weekly/fortnightly updates in English and Portuguese that provided an overview of individual incidents of violence, the observed trends, and the context of political violence in Cabo Delgado. As of 26 July 2023, Cabo Ligado shifted from publishing weekly updates to fortnightly updates due to the decrease in violence in the province, allowing for more time for indepth and highquality analysis. This change also enabled the team to allocate resources to produce a special actor profile series as noted below. The announcement of this change was wellreceived by Cabo Ligados key stakeholders, newsletter subscribers, and visitors to the Cabo Ligado website. A total of 47 weekly/fortnightly updates were published during the implementation period.Progress on Activity 2.1.2: From January 2023 to June 2024, the Cabo Ligado team of experts and analysts continued to publish monthly reports in English and Portuguese that provide a summary of political violence incidents occurring throughout the month, along with a number of reports that focus on the latest trends and developments in the conflict. The latter reports were informed by political developments in Mozambique, the expertise of guest writers, and CRs suggestions on topics that required further attention and investigation in their respective districts. As of October 2023, Cabo Ligado launched a new series of actor profile reports, providing an indepth overview and analysis of the key actors involved in Cabo Delgados complex conflict landscape. The Cabo Ligado teams focus on identifying the roles of state and nonstate actors across conflict theatres in East Africa that could reescalate violence in the country was well received by its key users and stakeholders.

title.narrative: Output 3.1 related to Objective 3: Key stakeholders are better informed on trends and dynamics related to political violence and protest in Mozambique through direct engagements and meetings.

description.narrative: Progress on Activity 3.1.1ACLED engaged with highlevel stakeholders through 59 inperson and remote meetings, providing analytical insights into the Cabo Delgado conflict and regional violence trends. These engagements fostered collaboration, enhanced security monitoring, and supported policymaking in Mozambique, with approximately 400 participants (including 38 women). Key engagements included:Workshop on Peacebuilding & Preventing Violent Extremism (June 2024, Pemba) Organized by GIZ and ADIN, with presentations on conflict trends, key actors, and forecasts. (66 participants)Meetings with Canadian & Norwegian Embassies (June & May 2024, Maputo & virtual) Discussed Cabo Ligados next phase and conflict updates. (8 participants total)Situational Update Briefing on Cabo Delgado (April 2024, virtual) Attended by 220 participants, including UN, EEAS, USAID, and the World Bank, discussing violence resurgence and forecasts. (226 participants)Briefing for UN Department of Peace Operations (March 2024) Covered ISM actor profiles, group development, and conflict trends. (8 participants)Portugal Embassy Seminar on Durable Solutions (Feb 2024, Pretoria) Provided analysis of insurgency trends and political violence. (Participants not specified)Engagement with US Embassy & USAID (Nov 2023 & June 2024, Maputo) Discussed ACLED data as a fragility indicator, human rights monitoring, and state behavior analysis. (9 participants total)Meetings with Norwegian Refugee Council, Save the Children, MSF, and WFP (Nov 2023, Maputo & Pemba) Addressed security trends, data integration for programming, misinformation, and IED use. (10 participants total)UNHCR Gender Unit Meeting (Nov 2023, Pemba) Explored genderbased violence data sharing and identification of female CRs. (2 participants)Embassy of Ireland Engagement (Nov 2023 & June 2024, Maputo) Discussed insurgency presence in national reserves and electionrelated security. (5 participants total)US State Department & USAID Briefing on Mozambique Conflict Data (Aug 2023, Washington, DC) Explained ACLED data use in monitoring political violence. (5 participants)Meetings with Netherlands Embassy & International Crisis Group (June 2023, Nairobi) Shared Cabo Ligado insights for policymaking and established communication channels. (10 participants total)Progress on Activity 3.1.2ACLEDs Cabo Ligado team directly engaged with EU stakeholders in 12 of the 59 external meetings, targeting entities such as EUTM Mozambique, the EU Delegation to Mozambique, and the FPI Regional Team in Nairobi. Key interactions included:EUTM Mozambique Briefings Conducted multiple inperson and virtual sessions throughout the grant period, facilitating almost daily communication for incident verification and updates on Mozambican forces actions.EU Delegation to Mozambique Provided regular conflict briefings, including a strategic review with EEAS in Nov 2023 and a closeddoor session in Feb 2024 on escalating violence and misconduct by Mozambican forces.FPI Regional Team in Nairobi Held multiple briefings discussing Cabo Ligado analysis and security trends.These engagements strengthened ACLEDs role in providing critical data for policymaking, security monitoring, and humanitarian response planning in Mozambique.

description.narrative: Progress on Activity 3.2.1: Cabo Ligado is a crucial resource for local organizations and communities in Cabo Delgado, through its podcast Voz de Cabo Delgado. The podcast episodes range from five to nine minutes in duration and bring independent, datadriven news and commentary on the Cabo Delgado conflict to listeners across Mozambique. Cabo Ligado consistently produced biweekly episodes in five languages (Portuguese, Kiswahili, Emakwa, Shimakonde, and Kimwani) during the implementation period. From January 2023 to June 2024, an average of 40 episodes were produced each month in all five languages. The podcast episodes are also hosted on the Cabo Ligado website.Progress on Activity 3.2.2: Podcast episodes are broadcast through Xipalapala, which distributes programming to a network of at least 29 community radio stations in the provinces of Northern and Central Mozambique, and Plural Medias iono.fm account, an online platform that promotes informative content about Mozambique in podcast and news formats. The Voz de Cabo Delgado episodes are also distributed more widely through various social media channels, including WhatsApp, Telegram, X, and Facebook. in all relevant languages. During the grant period, the Cabo Ligado team made efforts to expand the podcasts reach, further to the production of its `A Voz de Cabo Delgado Podcast Reach Strategy in March 2023, by improving its promotion strategy and expanding its presence on social media. Data from Plural Medias iono.fm account indicates that podcast episodes in all five languages received over 1,220 listens per month on average during the implementation period, with Portuguese episodes receiving the most attention, comprising half the monthly average listens. Additionally, the Voz de Cabo Delgado website attracts an average of more than 3,330 visitors monthly, with fluctuations reflecting developments on the ground. While radio listenership via Xipalapala lacks verifiable metrics, social media subscriber lists have grown during the reporting period. As of June 2024, Plural Medias X page had 1,235 followers, while the podcasts Facebook page had 440 followers. On Telegram, Voz de Cabo Delgado boasts 378 subscribers on the Portuguese channel, with varying numbers across other channels, and on WhatsApp, broadcast lists range from 1,633 on the Portuguese list to 9 on the Kimwani list. Additionally, WhatsApp channels were created in three languages Portuguese (725 subscribers), Shimakonde (20 subscribers), and Kiswahili (11 subscribers) to further expand the dissemination of podcast episodes to local organizations and communities in Mozambique.Feedback gathered from local communities and social media underscores the podcasts value, not only for HDP practitioners and other stakeholders but also for community members, particularly IDPs in the Cabo Delgado province. Despite limited internet access, those with connectivity share and listen to the podcasts together with those without internet access, aiding their understanding of the conflict dynamics and facilitating decisionmaking, such as assessing safety for returning to their areas of origin. Testimonials from displaced individuals from different districts highlight how the podcasts, offered in their native languages, enhance their understanding of conflict trends and the security situation on the ground, especially for those who cannot read. On WhatsApp, the platform with the highest subscriber count, users expressed gratitude for the insightful updates and analysis provided by Voz de Cabo Delgado, facilitated by the efforts of Plural Media and Cabo Ligado.
